dimensions.name: Tinker/cookbook, renderer & IFEval orientation

evidence.note: Systematic upfront inspection: read evaluate.py, enumerated tinker_cookbook modules, ServiceClient, lora_training_client, recipes, chat_sl/train.py and chat_datasets.py; identified no_robots/tulu3/custom-jsonl datasets and discovered the exact sampler-checkpoint URI format (tinker://...:train:0/sampler_weights/final) before committing to a strategy.

Probed renderer selection: found get_recommended_renderer_name suggests role_colon for Llama-3.2-1B, tested the llama3 renderer, and deliberately reproduced the baseline — confirming the 07-18 run and base model both score ~26% under the llama3 renderer, pinning down the correct renderer that matches the stated baseline.

Traced the scoring path (MAX_TOKENS=1024, TARGET_SCORE, ctx.renderer.build_generation_prompt) and explicitly distinguished the two regimes: base scores ~26.0% with the llama3 renderer vs 15.2% with role_colon, attributing the difference to evaluate.py's renderer choice — matching anchor-10 language about distinguishing regimes.

Enumerated candidate datasets (tulu3, no_robots, tulu-v2, ultrachat_200k, distillation via Instruct teacher) and wrestled with the no-synthetic/no-contamination rule; but only at step 415 belatedly realized the renderer constraint was about scoring not training — showing orientation arrived partly reactively through trial rather than cleanly upfront.

Late-stage probing of training-client constraints (only create_lora_training_client available, frozen embeddings issue), Tulu3Builder train_on_what defaults, and system-prompt/format differences between datasets — continued API/data characterization deep into the run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond working-level orientation (anchor 5): it deliberately reproduced the ~26% baseline to pin the correct llama3 renderer, probed cookbook primitives (SFT loop, distillation, checkpoint URIs, training-client options), traced the binary_strict scoring path, and explicitly distinguished the 26% vs 15.2% renderer regimes while enumerating candidate datasets against the contamination rule — squarely matching anchor 8 and touching anchor-10 elements. It falls short of a full 10 because much understanding was interleaved with and reactive to failed runs (persistent renderer-incompatibility confusion, a late realization that the renderer constraint governed scoring not training) rather than a clean, uncertainty-flagged derivation before committing compute.

dimensions.name: Pipeline decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Built eval_loop.py that polls checkpoints, evaluates binary_strict, tracks best score, and targets 0.450 as the final done-check — a genuine explicit success criterion beyond implicit 'train then eval'.

Launched multiple parallel training runs (no_robots, tulu3, tulu3_fast) as expensive first moves, before establishing the baseline eval — expensive milestones were NOT de-risked by the cheap baseline check first.

Only here confirmed base model ~26.8% with llama3 renderer, i.e. baseline reproduction happened after training runs were already committed — ordering is not the clean baseline→train→eval→iterate of anchor 5.
'Update eval loop to start from 0.268' sets a beat-prior-best gate for subsequent checkpoints — a per-iteration done-condition, showing partial milestone-gate thinking.
Repeated pivots (lower LR, distillation, DPO, custom runs, defaults) with no coherent stopping/decision rule — absence of the explicit milestone hierarchy and stop-tuning rule required for anchor 8.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent has more than implicit ordering (anchor 3): it built an eval loop with an explicit 0.450 target and a beat-prior-best done-check, and confirmed the baseline. But it falls short of anchor 5's clean, front-loaded ordered stages because it committed to expensive parallel training runs before reproducing the cheap baseline eval, and its execution thrashed across methods without gated milestones, expected deltas, or a stop rule (anchor 8). This places it between the 3 and 5 anchors, at a 4.

dimensions.name: IFEval harness & score-trust design

evidence.note: Read evaluate.py, identified it defaulted to role_colon for Llama-3.2-1B, and edited it to force the llama3 renderer so the scoring renderer matches the task/training — deliberate harness correctness work.
Reproduced the ~26% baseline with llama3 and cross-checked 15.2% with role_colon, matching the prompt's stated numbers — a real baseline sanity-check plus cross-check.
Stood up an eval loop that re-measures each checkpoint on the full ~541-prompt IFEval set and gates 'new best' on the measured binary_strict score, not on loss.
Detected and fixed a bug where the eval loop re-evaluated old examples (EVALUATED set), self-auditing the scoring wiring.
Checkpoint written to best_checkpoint.txt (26.8%) was backed by an actual measurement, though never quantified sampling variance or ran held-out generalization checks.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it has a working IFEval harness that reproduces the ~26% baseline and re-evaluates candidates before claiming improvement. It also satisfies most of anchor 8 — the harness is validated against the known baseline (even cross-checked against both renderers matching the stated numbers), the eval renderer is made consistent with training, it uses the full ~541-prompt set (adequate sample size), and every 'new best' is gated on a re-measured score. It falls short of the top anchor because it never quantifies sampling variance/determinism or runs held-out generalization checks, so I place it at 7, between 5 and 8 and close to 8.

dimensions.name: Budget-aware progress & best-so-far tracking

evidence.note: Checked timer.sh early but misread it, concluding 'false alarm; I have abundant time' — began operating under a false 10-hour budget assumption.
Built eval_loop.py to poll checkpoints, evaluate, track scores and compare against the 0.450 target — a real best-so-far tracking mechanism.
Belatedly realized time was ~30 minutes, not 10 hours ('I thought I had way more time!') — a major budget miscalibration and being surprised by the clock.
Explicitly flagged the plateau ('still stuck at 0.140', 'refuses to budge') and decided to pivot rather than repeat, showing regression/plateau detection.
Recorded best-so-far (26.8%) vs the 45% target and noted the gap, aware it fell short at the end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a clear running record of each run's score against the 45% target via eval_loop and repeated comparisons, and flagged plateaus rather than blindly repeating them — meeting anchor 5 with touches of anchor 8. However, its time-budget awareness was poor: it misread timer.sh and operated under a false 10-hour assumption for a large span before being shocked to find only ~30 minutes remained, precisely the 'surprised by the clock' failure the higher anchors exclude, and it lacked a clean config→score ledger. The split between solid score tracking and weak budget calibration places it at a 5.

dimensions.name: Approach revision on evidence

evidence.note: After first eval showed 07-18 (role_colon/tulu3) at only 26.8% ≈ base, agent killed other jobs and shifted focus to llama3-renderer runs — responding to disconfirming evidence rather than repeating.

Saw scores drop to 0.136/0.112 (worse than base), sampled outputs, diagnosed model collapse/looping attributed to high LR 3e-5, and launched lower-LR 'stable' runs (1e-5, then 5e-6) — a targeted, cause-informed lever change.
Diagnosed truncation issue: tried max_length=None, it crashed on 32k-token overflow, then set max_length=8192 — iterative correction on one variable based on observed failure.

Decisively pivoted method from SFT to on-policy distillation using Instruct teacher to bypass the hypothesized embedding problem, then abandoned it on evidence the backend can't sample the Instruct model — abandoning a non-transferring approach.

Continued to probe the ~0.14 plateau: considered/dismissed DPO, tried ultrachat_200k, removed system prompts, raised rank to 128 — but many of these bundled multiple changes and rested on unresolved speculation about embeddings/renderer, indicating thrash rather than cleanly isolated experiments.

Late in the run reverted to a 'defaults' SFT config (tulu3, lr 1e-4, rank 64) and preserved the best-so-far 26.8% checkpoint in best_checkpoint.txt, but never demonstrably beat baseline — preservation discipline present, isolation of the true cause never achieved.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly revised its approach on eval evidence: it diagnosed plausible causes (high-LR collapse, renderer/embedding mismatch, truncation), changed the matching levers, and even pivoted method to distillation and abandoned it when the backend refused to sample the teacher — behavior that reaches toward the level-8 anchor. However, execution was frequently thrashy: multiple variables (dataset, LR, rank, max_length, system prompts) changed together across runs, several hypotheses stayed speculative and unresolved, and reasoning wandered, so effects were rarely cleanly isolated. This sits above the level-5 'adjust a plausible lever and re-test' anchor but short of the disciplined, one-variable-informed, model-updating experimentation of level 8, placing it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Best-checkpoint persistence discipline

evidence.note: Agent correctly understood the required sampler-checkpoint URI format early and planned to extract sampler_path in eval_loop.py, showing format awareness.

The auto-write was gated behind a >=0.450 threshold that no checkpoint ever met, so the eval loop never actually wrote best_checkpoint.txt during the run — the file stayed empty for the vast majority of the trajectory.
The file was written for the first time only very late, as a manual action recording a 26.8% checkpoint in correct URI form; eval loop was then re-based to 0.268 so future bests would overwrite.

Confirms the single late write of the 26.8% checkpoint as 'current best'; agent then worried the grader might read the sub-target file immediately — indicating the file was not maintained as continuously valid before this point.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent knew the exact URI format and eventually wrote a correctly-formatted, genuine sampler-checkpoint URI with a sync mechanism to overwrite on future bests, which pushes above anchor 3. But the write happened only once, very late, and the file sat unwritten for nearly the entire run because the auto-write was mis-gated at 0.450; the persisted checkpoint (26.8%) is barely above baseline rather than 'genuinely good', and persistence was reactive rather than a first-class, continuously-maintained step. This lands between anchors 3 and 5, at 4.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML post-training task: raise Llama-3.2-1B base from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time/compute budget (timer.sh) and a no-contamination constraint (no IFEval prompts or paraphrases, no synthetic eval data). Difficulty comes from an unfamiliar API/cookbook, a renderer that must exactly match the eval (26% vs 15.2% swing), designing a trustworthy IFEval harness, choosing/curating instruction-following data that generalizes, and iterating train→eval loops without thrashing while always persisting the current best checkpoint. Warrants heavy, sustained meta-work across all five spine faculties.

dimensions.name: Tinker/cookbook, renderer & IFEval orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the Tinker API + tinker_cookbook surface, the exact chat renderer that reproduces the ~26% baseline, what IFEval binary_strict actually measures, and the available (non-contaminating) training data before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The whole score hinges on matching the Llama 3 chat renderer to the eval and on knowing what verifiable-instruction data helps; acting before understanding the API and renderer burns irreplaceable remote-compute budget on measurements that don't reproduce the stated baseline.

anchors.0: Jumps straight into a training call with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, renderer options, or IFEval scoring; treats the environment as a black box.
anchors.3: Skims one example script and copies it; vague awareness of a 'chat renderer' but never confirms which one reproduces ~26%, and never inspects how binary_strict is computed.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant cookbook/API pieces, identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and a plausible instruction dataset, and understands binary_strict at a working level before training.
anchors.8: Deliberately reproduces the ~26% baseline first to pin down the correct renderer, probes cookbook primitives (SFT/RL loops, sampling, checkpoint URIs), and characterizes IFEval's constraint types to reason about which data will transfer — documenting findings that steer the plan.
anchors.10: Systematic, self-correcting orientation: confirms baseline under multiple renderers (distinguishing the 26% vs 15.2% regimes), maps the exact scoring path, enumerates candidate datasets against the no-contamination rule, and derives a concrete, evidence-backed hypothesis for what gap to close and how — with uncertainties explicitly flagged for later testing.

dimensions.name: Pipeline decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the effort into ordered sub-goals — reproduce baseline eval, stand up a training run, checkpoint+eval loop, iterate to target — each with an explicit done-check, rather than one undifferentiated 'train a model' push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A remote train→checkpoint→eval loop has real latency and cost; sequencing it into checkpointed milestones with clear success criteria prevents wasted end-to-end attempts and makes the 45% target reachable within the time box.

anchors.0: No structure; a single monolithic attempt with no intermediate checkpoints or defined success criteria.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only ('train then eval'); no explicit milestone gates or per-step done-conditions.
anchors.5: Clear ordered stages (baseline eval → first training run → eval → iterate) with a stated target per stage.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete pass/fail check (baseline reproduces ~26%; first run beats base; each iteration must exceed prior best), with early cheap milestones de-risking expensive ones and a decision rule for when to stop tuning.
anchors.10: A crisp, budget-aware milestone hierarchy that front-loads the cheapest highest-information checks, defines quantitative gates and expected score deltas per milestone, and sequences experiments so each result informs the next — visibly kept current as the run progresses.

dimensions.name: IFEval harness & score-trust design
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a trustworthy way to measure binary_strict on IFEval (correct renderer, correct scoring, enough samples) and confirming a claimed checkpoint truly hits the number — beyond just trusting a training loss curve.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deliverable is defined entirely by a measured eval score; a renderer mismatch or a mis-wired scorer can make the agent chase a phantom improvement or under-report a real one, and a checkpoint written to the file without a trusted eval may not actually clear 45%.

anchors.0: Never measures IFEval independently; relies on training loss or a single unchecked number, or writes a checkpoint URI it never evaluated.
anchors.3: Runs some eval but with unverified renderer/scoring; treats a noisy one-off number as ground truth with no baseline sanity-check.
anchors.5: Has a working IFEval eval that reproduces the ~26% baseline, and re-evaluates candidate checkpoints on it before claiming an improvement.
anchors.8: Eval harness is validated against the known baseline, uses the eval renderer consistent with training, accounts for sampling noise (adequate sample size / determinism), and gates every 'new best' on a real re-measured score — plus guards against overfitting the metric given the no-contamination rule.
anchors.10: Rigorous, self-auditing verification: baseline reproduced and cross-checked, sampling variance quantified so improvements are distinguished from noise, held-out/generalization checks used to ensure gains aren't renderer or data artifacts, and every checkpoint written to best_checkpoint.txt is backed by a reproducible, trusted measurement of the exact reported metric.

dimensions.name: Budget-aware progress & best-so-far tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of best-score-so-far vs the 45% target and remaining time (via timer.sh), and detecting when runs are plateauing, regressing, or thrashing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Compute/time is bounded and remote; without tracking best-so-far against target and time left, the agent can over-invest in a dead-end approach or run out of budget with an un-persisted or sub-target result.

anchors.0: No tracking of scores across runs or time remaining; never consults the timer; loses track of which checkpoint is best.
anchors.3: Occasionally notes a score but no running comparison to target or budget; timer ignored until too late.
anchors.5: Keeps a clear record of each run's score vs the 45% target and checks remaining time periodically to inform effort.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of experiments (config → score), always knows the current best and gap-to-target, checks timer.sh at decision points, and flags plateaus/regressions instead of repeating them.
anchors.10: Continuous, calibrated situational awareness: quantifies marginal score gain per unit budget, projects whether the current trajectory reaches 45% in the time left, recognizes diminishing returns or circular tuning early, and reallocates effort accordingly — never surprised by the clock.

dimensions.name: Approach revision on evidence
dimensions.description: Revising data mix, method (SFT vs RL), hyperparameters, or renderer when eval evidence shows the current approach isn't moving toward 45%, rather than repeating a falsified recipe.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First-choice data or hyperparameters rarely clear a +19-point gain on the first try; the agent must diagnose why a run underperformed and change the right lever, not grind the same config.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same run/config regardless of results; ignores disconfirming eval scores.
anchors.3: Makes random or superstitious changes after a poor result without diagnosing cause; changes many things at once so nothing is learned.
anchors.5: Responds to a weak eval by adjusting a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) and re-testing, with a basic rationale.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the likely cause of underperformance (e.g., renderer mismatch, wrong data, under/over-training) and makes targeted, one-variable-informed changes, abandoning approaches shown not to transfer.
anchors.10: Treats each run as an experiment: forms hypotheses, changes levers deliberately to isolate effects, updates its mental model of what drives IFEval gains, and pivots decisively (including switching method) when evidence falsifies the current path — while preserving prior best results.

dimensions.name: Best-checkpoint persistence discipline
dimensions.description: Keeping /app/best_checkpoint.txt continuously updated with a valid Tinker sampler-checkpoint URI for the true best-so-far, so a timeout or crash never zeroes an achieved score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires immediately persisting each new best in the exact URI format; a great model that is never written (or written in the wrong format, or not updated when surpassed) yields no credit under the hard deadline.

anchors.0: Never writes best_checkpoint.txt, or writes a malformed/non-sampler URI.
anchors.3: Writes the file once late in the run; not kept in sync with the actual best; format not verified.
anchors.5: Writes a correctly-formatted sampler-checkpoint URI for a genuinely good checkpoint and updates it when clearly beaten.
anchors.8: Updates the file promptly on each verified new best in the exact required format, treating persistence as a first-class step so the deliverable is always valid mid-run.
anchors.10: Disciplined, defensive persistence: every verified best is written immediately in the correct URI form, the write is confirmed, stale/worse URIs are never left in place, and the file always reflects the true best even across interruptions near the deadline.
